title: Aortic stenosis (adult): assessment and timing of intervention
subject: cardiology
summary: Severe AS is mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, Vmax 4.0 m/s or more and AVA 1.0 cm2 or less; intervene when symptomatic or LVEF is below 50%, consider early intervention if asymptomatic at low risk, with TAVI at 70 years or older and SAVR below 70 at low surgical risk (ESC/EACTS 2025).

sections.title: Recognise
items: Symptoms: exertional breathlessness, angina, exertional dizziness or syncope, and falling exercise tolerance. Once symptoms appear, prognosis without valve intervention is poor.
Signs: slow-rising low-volume pulse, ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, soft or absent second heart sound, narrow pulse pressure. The murmur can soften as the ventricle fails.
Causes: age-related calcific degeneration in older adults, bicuspid valve in younger adults (look for aortopathy), and rheumatic disease (usually with mitral involvement).
Transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis may coexist in older patients (low flow, thick walls, carpal tunnel syndrome): exclude a monoclonal protein and confirm with bone scintigraphy.
Decompensated severe AS presents as pulmonary oedema, syncope or low-output state; the patient is preload dependent and tolerates hypotension poorly.

sections.title: Echo grading and further tests
items: Severe high-gradient AS: mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, Vmax 4.0 m/s or more, AVA 1.0 cm2 or less (indexed 0.6 cm2/m2 or less), severe regardless of LV function or flow. Moderate AS: AVA 1.0 to 1.5 cm2 (or mean gradient 25 to 40 mmHg) with normal flow.

Discordant results: first exclude measurement error (LVOT diameter, multi-window Doppler) and reversible high flow (anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, AV fistula) or low flow (bradycardia, uncontrolled hypertension).

Low-flow, low-gradient AS (AVA 1.0 cm2 or less, mean gradient below 40 mmHg, stroke volume index 35 mL/m2 or less): with LVEF below 50%, dobutamine stress echo (flow reserve = stroke volume rise of 20% or more) separates true severe from pseudo-severe AS.

CT aortic valve calcium score supports severe AS when findings are discordant: above 2000 Agatston units in men and above 1200 in women (less reliable in bicuspid, rheumatic or radiation-damaged valves).
Apparently asymptomatic severe AS: exercise testing (if feasible) can unmask symptoms or a sustained BP fall of more than 20 mmHg. Do not exercise-test symptomatic patients.
Also: ECG, BNP or NT-proBNP, coronary assessment before intervention (CT coronary angiography or invasive angiography), and cardiac CT to plan TAVI (annulus size, femoral access, coronary heights).

sections.title: Indications for intervention
items: Symptomatic severe high-gradient AS: intervention recommended (class I) when life expectancy exceeds about 1 year.

Symptomatic low-flow, low-gradient AS with LVEF below 50%: intervene after confirming true severe AS (dobutamine stress echo or CT calcium score). With LVEF 50% or more: intervention should be considered after careful confirmation.
Asymptomatic severe AS with LVEF below 50% and no other cause: intervention recommended.

Asymptomatic severe high-gradient AS with LVEF 50% or more (normal exercise test if feasible): early intervention should be considered as an alternative to close surveillance if procedural risk is low (class IIa, level A).

The case for early intervention is stronger with very severe AS (mean gradient 60 mmHg or more, or Vmax above 5.0 m/s), severe calcification with Vmax rise of 0.3 m/s per year or more, BNP more than 3 times the age- and sex-corrected normal, LVEF below 55%, or a sustained BP fall above 20 mmHg on exercise.
Moderate AS: operate only when the patient is already having CABG, aortic or other valve surgery.

sections.title: Choice of procedure and medical care
items: Decide the mode of intervention in a Heart Team at a Heart Valve Centre, using age, life expectancy, anatomy, surgical risk (STS-PROM, EuroSCORE II) and lifetime management.

TAVI recommended at 70 years or older with a tricuspid aortic valve and suitable anatomy (transfemoral route preferred). SAVR recommended below 70 years when surgical risk is low (STS-PROM and EuroSCORE II below 4%).
Bicuspid valve stenosis: SAVR is usual; TAVI may be considered at increased surgical risk with suitable anatomy.
Balloon aortic valvotomy may be used as a bridge in haemodynamically unstable patients or before urgent high-risk non-cardiac surgery.
No drug slows progression (statins do not). Treat hypertension, preferably with an ACE inhibitor or ARB, titrated cautiously to avoid symptomatic hypotension.
Heart failure with severe AS: diuretics cautiously for congestion, but do not let temporary symptomatic improvement delay intervention.
After TAVI without another indication for anticoagulation: aspirin 75 to 100 mg daily for 12 months, then long-term aspirin should be considered. Routine DAPT or anticoagulation is not recommended.

sections.title: Follow-up
items: Asymptomatic severe AS under surveillance: review at least every 6 months (symptoms, echo, natriuretic peptide), and immediately if symptoms appear.
Moderate AS, especially with significant calcification: at least yearly. Mild AS without significant calcification in younger patients: every 2 to 3 years.
Teach patients to report breathlessness, chest pain, dizziness or syncope promptly rather than waiting for the next appointment.
After valve replacement: echo within the first weeks as a baseline, then yearly clinical and echo review of bioprostheses, and whenever symptoms change.

sections.title: Special situations
items: Non-cardiac surgery: urgent low or intermediate risk surgery can proceed under strict haemodynamic monitoring. For elective high-risk surgery with symptoms or LV dysfunction, the Heart Team decides on TAVI or SAVR first.
Anaesthesia and acute care: avoid hypotension, tachycardia and abrupt vasodilatation (for example high-dose nitrates or dense neuraxial block); treat hypotension promptly with a vasoconstrictor.
Endocarditis prophylaxis before dental procedures that manipulate the gingiva or periapical region is indicated after valve replacement (including TAVI), not for native AS alone.
Pregnancy: counsel before conception; symptomatic severe AS should be treated before pregnancy.
In India, rheumatic and bicuspid disease are relatively more common in younger patients; the strongest TAVI evidence is in tricuspid calcific AS, so involve an experienced Heart Team.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Calling low-gradient AS moderate without checking stroke volume index, LVEF and the calcium score.
Attributing breathlessness to age or deconditioning in a sedentary patient; use exercise testing or natriuretic peptides.
Giving large doses of nitrates or vasodilators, or over-diuresing, in severe AS (sudden hypotension and collapse).
Missing coexisting coronary disease or cardiac amyloidosis before intervention.

drugs.name: Aspirin (after TAVI)
drugs.dose: 75 to 100 mg orally once daily for 12 months, then long-term should be considered
drugs.notes: Patients without an indication for oral anticoagulation. Routine DAPT is not recommended.

drugs.name: Furosemide
drugs.dose: 20 to 40 mg orally or IV, titrated to congestion
drugs.notes: Use cautiously: excessive diuresis reduces preload and can cause hypotension.

drugs.name: Ramipril
drugs.dose: Start 1.25 to 2.5 mg orally once daily, titrate slowly
drugs.notes: For coexisting hypertension; avoid symptomatic hypotension. Check potassium and creatinine.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin (endocarditis prophylaxis)
drugs.dose: 2 g orally 30 to 60 minutes before the dental procedure
drugs.notes: Only for prosthetic valves (including TAVI) and other high-risk groups. Penicillin allergy: azithromycin or clarithromycin 500 mg, or doxycycline 100 mg.
